sentences.text: Mantellisaurus honors Gideon Mantell, the discoverer of Iguanodon, and was a lightly constructed iguanodontian dinosaur. It reached a length of 7 meters and a weight of 750 kilograms, though some estimates suggest it was smaller than Iguanodon bernissartensis.
The forelimbs of Mantellisaurus were proportionally shorter than those of Iguanodon bernissartensis.
A significant specimen, IRSNB 1551, became the second mounted non-avian dinosaur skeleton made primarily of actual bone when displayed by Louis Dollo in 1884.
Gideon Mantell purchased a Maidstone specimen for £25 in June 1834 and identified it as an Iguanodon based on its distinctive teeth.
Fossil remains of Mantellisaurus have been found in Belgium, England, Spain, and Germany. The genus contains only one species, Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis.

The holotype specimen was discovered by Reginald Walter Hooley in 1914 in southern England and reported in 1917. Reginald Walter Hooley named the species Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1925, after his death. The species name 'atherfieldensis' refers to the village of Atherfield on the Isle of Wight where the fossil was found.

In 1971, a quarry near Nehden, Germany, yielded numerous disarticulated iguanodontid remains, mostly Mantellisaurus, alongside other dinosaur and crocodylian fragments. Mantellisaurus fossils are known from several localities in Spain, including an articulated hindlimb from Las Hoyas and a specimen from Rubielos de Mora. Three Mantellisaurus specimens are known from the Arcillas de Morella Formation in Spain.
Gregory Paul proposed that Mantellisaurus was primarily bipedal, using all fours only when standing still or moving slowly.
Gregory Paul established the genus Mantellisaurus in 2007, separating it from Iguanodon atherfieldensis. Gregory S. Paul recognized Mantellisaurus as a distinct dinosaur genus in 2006.

Mantellisaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically from the Barremian to the early Aptian ages. However, other sources record the time range from the Berriasian to the Aptian, spanning from 143.1 to 119.57 million years ago.

A Belgian specimen was originally assigned to Iguanodon mantelli in 1881 but was later thought to belong to Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1986. Gregory S. Paul assigned this specimen to the genus and species Dollodon bampingi in 2008. In 2010, Kenneth Carpenter and Yusuke Ishida synonymized Dollodon bampingi with Iguanodon seelyi.

The validity of the genus Dollodon is disputed among researchers. In 2012, Andrew McDonald considered Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis to be a synonym of Dollodon bampingi and possibly Proplanicoxa galtoni. The validity of the genus Dollodon has been disputed since its description.
